parts.title: Catering for a school summer fair
parts.context: A parent phones a catering company to arrange food for a school summer fair.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a catering company to arrange food for a school summer fair. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Good morning, Larkspur Catering, Dev speaking.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, hello. I'm phoning about food for our school's summer fair. A friend of mine said you did the catering at her daughter's school.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Yes, we do a lot of school events. I'll take a few details first, and then we can talk about what you need.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman is arranging food for a summer fair, so 'summer fair' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Right, could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, it's Helen Fairbrother.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Sorry, could you spell the surname for me?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Of course. It's F-A-I-R-B-R-O-T-H-E-R.
script.tts: Of course. It's F, A, I, R, B, R, O, T, H, E, R.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Thank you. And are you one of the teachers at the school?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, no, I'm just a parent. But I chair the Parents' Association this year, so the food is left to me.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Lovely. And when is the fair?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: It's on Saturday the 19th of June. Oh, sorry, no, that was last year's date. This year it's the 26th.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: The 26th, fine. And roughly how many people are you expecting?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Well, about 200 came last year, but we've advertised in the local paper this time, so we're hoping for 250.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Will everything be outdoors?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The stalls and the games will be on the school field, yes. But you know what the weather's like here, so we'd like the food to be under cover somewhere, if that's possible.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: It is. I'd recommend a marquee. We can put one up next to the field for you, and it only costs a little extra.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, that would be perfect. Last year the food was in the hall, and it was a long way from everything else.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Now, what sort of food were you thinking of?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Well, last year we had a barbecue, but it rained all afternoon and the poor volunteers got soaked, so I'd rather not do that again.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: I don't blame you. We could do a baked potato bar, with different fillings, or a selection of wraps and salads.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Hmm. Potatoes might get a bit messy with the little ones, don't you think? Let's go for the wraps.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Lovely. Do you have any dietary requirements we should know about?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, one important thing. As far as I know, nobody has a problem with dairy or gluten, but three of the children have serious allergies, so there mustn't be any nuts in anything.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: That's no trouble. We don't use them in our wraps anyway.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Thank you. And how much would it all cost? Our budget's quite tight.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Normally the wrap lunch is 8 pounds per person, but we give schools a discount, so for you it would be 6 pounds, and that includes a drink.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, that's better than I'd hoped.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: And how would you like to pay? I can send an invoice to the school office, or you could pay by card on the day.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: An invoice, please. The school secretary deals with all of that.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Fine. Now, the delivery. Our van will arrive at about nine o'clock. Should the driver come in by the main gate, on Station Road?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, no, that will be closed because of the children's parade. Could he come round to the back gate, in Mill Lane?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: The back gate, in Mill Lane. Fine, I've made a note. I'll email you a quote this afternoon.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Thank you so much. You've been really helpful.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A visit to a lighthouse
parts.context: A guide leads a group of visitors round a coastal lighthouse and visitor centre.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a talk to a group of visitors at a lighthouse and visitor centre. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Skerrow Point Lighthouse. My name's Ewan, and I'll be showing you round today. First, let me explain how the site is laid out, so please look at the map on your sheet. We're standing at the bottom, just inside the main entrance, in front of the visitor centre.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: First, refreshments. The tearoom is the small building immediately to the right of the visitor centre, the one with the bright blue door. The toilets are on the other side, between the visitor centre and the car park, so do use them before we start, because there aren't any further up.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Now, the path straight ahead of us leads up to the lighthouse, and about halfway up it crosses the cliff path, which runs from left to right on your map. If you turn right at the crossing and follow the cliff path, the first building you come to, set back a little on the right, is the fog signal station. A huge horn in there used to warn ships in foggy weather, and you can still see the old machinery.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Carry on to the very end of the path, and you'll find the coastguard lookout, on your left, right on the edge of the cliff. It's a wonderful place to watch the seabirds, but please stay behind the rope.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Now, if we go back to the crossing and this time turn left, you'll pass a row of cottages on your left. They were built for the keepers' families, and now they house a small museum. At the far end of the row there's a little stone hut, which people often take to be part of the museum. In fact it's the old oil store, and it's kept locked for safety.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Then, opposite the cottages, on the right, you'll see the walled garden, where our volunteers grow herbs for the tearoom.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Right, that's the layout. Now a little about the lighthouse itself. People assume it was built to guide the fishing boats into Port Gannet, just around the headland. A reasonable guess, but the fishermen knew these waters perfectly well. The real reason was a reef called the Teeth, which lies half a mile offshore and vanishes completely at high tide. In 1861 a cargo steamer struck it in a storm, and a proper light was agreed. Until then there'd only been a coal fire in an iron basket on the cliff.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: The keepers took turns to look after the lamp, day and night, all year round. You might imagine the storms were the worst part, but they soon got used to those. The heavy work was tiring too, especially carrying cans of paraffin up all those steps. But the keepers' diaries show that what they dreaded most was the long night watches in winter, when it was all they could do to keep awake until dawn.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Now, a word about the climb. There are 147 steps to the top. I'm afraid we can't go into the lantern room today, where the great lens is. Normally it's closed only when the wind is very strong, and there's hardly a breath of it today. It holds just eight people at a time, but we could easily go up in groups. No, the reason this time is that an engineer is repairing part of the mechanism that turns the lens. So we'll climb as far as the watch room instead.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Your ticket money helps to pay for the upkeep of the site. The tower was repainted last year, thanks to a grant, and we'd love to build a classroom for school visits one day. But the first call on every ticket is the cliff path, where the edge near the lookout is crumbling into the sea.

script.speaker: ewan
script.text: Finally, in winter we run evening tours, when the lamp is switched on. You can't book at the desk here, because they always sell out weeks ahead, and the telephone line is only staffed on weekday mornings, so the quickest way is the website. Right, if there are no questions, let's make a start.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A study of tablets in primary classrooms
parts.context: Two education students discuss their study with a tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Amara and Ben, discussing a study of tablet computers in primary classrooms with their tutor, Dr Hargreaves. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Come in, both of you. I've read the draft of your tablet study, and it's coming along well. Remind me why you chose this topic. I have a feeling it came from one of my lectures.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Not this time, I'm afraid. I'd read an article about it over the summer, but that wasn't what decided us.

script.speaker: amara
script.text: No, it was my placement, really. The school where I was working had just bought thirty tablets, and when I arrived they were sitting in a cupboard, because nobody was sure how to use them in lessons.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: I see. And was it difficult to get the study started?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Not as much as we expected. The parents returned the consent forms within a week, and the teachers were keen to help. The real headache was the timetable. Between assemblies, music and swimming, finding six weeks of regular lessons took us ages.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Yes, schools are always crowded. So how did the study itself work?

script.speaker: amara
script.text: One Year 4 class used tablets in lessons for six weeks, while the parallel class carried on as usual. We observed the lessons and gave both classes the same test before and after.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: And how did the pupils feel about using them?

script.speaker: amara
script.text: In the first week or two they were thrilled. But by week four the novelty had worn off, and the teacher said she had to work much harder to keep them interested.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: We'd expected the boys to enjoy it more than the girls, but there was no real difference.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: And the test results? Did the tablets make a difference?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Less than we'd hoped. The tablet class went up a little more, but the gap was tiny. Both classes improved by almost the same amount.

script.speaker: amara
script.text: Not that the other class did any better, though.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Now, in your conclusion you say that tablets make no difference to learning in primary schools. I'd be careful there. With only fifty-two pupils from a single school, you shouldn't claim more than your evidence allows. And there's no need to recommend buying more tablets, either. But do keep the pupils' comments in. They're the most interesting part.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Right, now the section on how the tablets were used. Let's take the five activities one at a time. Starting with the maths game?

script.speaker: amara
script.text: It was the most successful. The game marks every answer straight away, so she wasn't taking home piles of exercise books. She reckoned that gave her two hours a week back. We'd worried the pupils would sneak off to play other games, but they stayed on task.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: And the reading app?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That was a surprise. We assumed the children would love reading on screen, but most of them preferred real books.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: What about the story-making project?

script.speaker: amara
script.text: That was my favourite. The pupils combined drawings, text and recorded voices, and the finished stories were far better than anything they'd written on paper. I'd expected it to help the weaker writers most, but the confident ones gained just as much.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: And the science quiz tool? I gather you had some difficulties.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: We did. In theory it was great. But the school network kept dropping out, and in two lessons the teacher spent half the time trying to reconnect everyone.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: And finally, the video recording?

script.speaker: amara
script.text: That worked brilliantly. The pupils filmed their own experiments in groups, and they kept supporting each other, deciding together who would film and who would explain.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: That's very good. Send me the next draft by Friday, and we'll talk again then.

script.speaker: amara
script.text: Thank you, Dr Hargreaves.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: why Roman concrete has lasted so long
parts.context: A lecture about the materials and methods behind Roman concrete.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about why Roman concrete has lasted so long. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at a puzzle in the history of engineering. Many Roman harbours, bridges and temples are still standing after two thousand years, yet a modern concrete road may start to crumble within fifty. So what did the Romans know that we have forgotten? To answer that, I'll begin with what their concrete was made of, then look at some of their most famous structures, and finish with some very recent research.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Modern concrete is based on cement, which was only invented in the nineteenth century. The Romans used something different. Their key ingredient was lime, which they mixed not with ordinary sand, as you might expect, but with volcanic ash. The best ash came from the region around Naples, and the Roman writer Vitruvius advised builders to use it wherever they could. To this paste they added the coarse material that gives concrete its bulk. Usually this was pieces of stone, though broken tiles were used as well, so that nothing went to waste.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Romans didn't only use concrete on land. They were among the first people to use it in the sea. All around the Mediterranean, they built harbours by pouring the mixture into huge wooden frames and lowering them into the water. Modern engineers would expect seawater to damage concrete, but when researchers examined samples drilled from ancient harbour walls, they found the opposite. Seawater had seeped slowly into the mixture, reacted with the ash, and caused tiny crystals to grow inside the concrete. These crystals locked the material together, so in a sense the concrete became stronger over the centuries, instead of weaker.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Of course, the best-known Roman concrete structure isn't a harbour at all. You might expect me to say the Colosseum, but the building I have in mind is the Pantheon in Rome, which was completed in about the year 126. Its dome is forty-three metres across, and it is still the largest dome in the world built from concrete without any steel inside it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The builders were extremely clever in the way they used their materials. At the base of the dome, they mixed in heavy rock to carry the load, but as the dome rose they switched to pumice, a volcanic rock so light that it can float on water. And the shell itself becomes thinner as it rises. It's about six metres thick near the bottom, but barely more than a metre at the top.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now compare that with a modern building. Today, concrete is almost always reinforced with steel bars, which gives it great strength, but also a weakness. Once water reaches the steel, it begins to rust, and because rust takes up more space than the metal, it pushes outwards and splits the concrete. That is why many modern structures need major repairs after fifty or sixty years. The Romans had no steel, and so, no rust.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: I'd like to end with the most surprising discovery of all. If you look closely at a piece of Roman concrete, you often see small white lumps scattered through it. They are made of lime, and for a long time experts assumed they were the result of careless mixing, a sign that the workers hadn't stirred the ingredients thoroughly. A recent research team has argued that exactly the opposite is true. The lumps act as a kind of repair kit. When a crack opens up, water seeps in and reaches the lumps. The lime dissolves, flows into the gap, and then hardens again into limestone, which seals the crack. In other words, the concrete can heal itself.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So the secret of Roman concrete was a combination of things: an unusual ingredient, a clever choice of materials, and, quite possibly, a built-in repair system. Engineers today are trying to copy these ideas, and next week we'll look at how they're getting on.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
